title: Before the Startup: six counterintuitive lessons for would-be founders
summary: Paul Graham explains why startups defy instinct and how to prepare. Expertise in your users and problem beats expertise in startup mechanics. Gaming the system stops working; only making something people want matters. Good ideas come from learning deeply and following interesting problems, not from brainstorming startup ideas.

principles.text: Startups are counterintuitive, so don't blindly trust your instincts about them.
principles.quote: But whatever the reason, starting a startup is a task where you can't always trust your instincts.

principles.text: Be an expert on your users and their problem, not on startup mechanics.
principles.quote: The way to succeed in a startup is not to be an expert on startups, but to be an expert on your users and the problem you're solving for them.

principles.text: Gaming the system stops working in a startup. Users only care whether the product does what they want.
principles.quote: So this is the third counterintuitive thing to remember about startups: starting a startup is where gaming the system stops working.

principles.text: Growth and fundraising both come down to making something people want.
principles.quote: And we have to tell them the best way to do that is simply to make something people want.

principles.text: A product users love beats fundraising tricks and a flat usage graph.
principles.quote: A founder who knows nothing about fundraising but has made something users love will have an easier time raising money than one who knows every trick in the book but has a flat usage graph.

principles.text: Don't try to think of startup ideas; become the kind of person who stumbles onto them.
principles.quote: that the way to get startup ideas is not to try to think of startup ideas.
